import type { Post } from "@/types/post";

export const samplePosts: Post[] = [
  {
    id: "heavy-industrial-capacity-update-2026q3",
    slug: "heavy-industrial-capacity-update-2026q3",
    title:
      "Update: China Takes 72% of H1 Ship Orders (+20 pp vs Completions) as Steel Midyear Share Rebounds to 53.7%",
    excerpt:
      "Versus our Aug update (91% Asia trio GT / 52% China steel), Clarksons H1 2026 puts China at 72% of newbuilding CGT orders and 65% of the end-June orderbook, while World Steel???s midyear run-rate lifts China???s crude share to 53.7%. Dry docks and the six-shop forge club stay frozen.",
    category: "Industry",
    themeId: "heavy-industrial-capacity",
    imageUrl:
      "/images/industry-heavy-industrial-capacity-update-2026q3-hero.png",
    imageAlt:
      "Dark navy cinematic shipyard dry dock with gantry cranes, welding glow, and teal-crimson concentration bars ??? Q3 heavy industrial capacity orderbook update",
    publishedAt: "2026-08-21T10:00:00Z",
    featured: true,
    visualization: "heavy-industrial-capacity-update-2026q3",
    layout: "default",
    content: `## What changed since the August completions update

Our [August heavy industrial capacity update](/blog/heavy-industrial-capacity-update-2026) answered the *completions and annual steel* question: UNCTADstat???s June 2026 insight put **91%** of 2025 GT completions in the China???Korea???Japan trio (**???4.2 pp** versus the research peak), World Steel???s 2025 totals cut China???s crude share to **52.0%**, and Cirium???s H1 wrap showed Airbus at **54%** of the Airbus+Boeing duo. Dry docks (~**62%** China among tracked VLCC-capable yards) and the **six-shop** ultra-heavy forge club were held. That post was a *backward-looking vintage*. This Q3 note is a *forward-capacity* delta.

Three mid-year prints force the rewrite. **Clarksons Research** shows China taking **72%** of global newbuilding orders by compensated gross tonnage in **H1 2026** ??? roughly **+20 percentage points** above the derived China weight inside the Aug update???s 2025 completions frame (~**52%**). Korea takes **19%** of H1 orders. The end-June **orderbook** puts China at **65%** of world CGT backlog (**134.03** of **206.59** million CGT). Separately, the **World Steel Association???s June 2026** release puts China at **500.0 Mt** of crude steel in H1 (**???3.0% YoY**) against **931.5 Mt** for reporting countries ??? a midyear share of **~53.7%**, **+1.7 pp** versus the FY2025 annual **52.0%**. Aircraft tempo also moved a notch: OEM July year-to-date deliveries put Airbus at **418** and Boeing at **367** (**53.2%** of the duo), **???0.8 pp** from Cirium???s H1 **54%**.

What did *not* move remains the industrial punchline. Tracked **VLCC-capable dry docks** stay China-heavy at ~**62%**. The **six-shop** RPV-class forge inventory is unchanged ??? still **zero** North American members. Completions-era Asia trio **91%** is also held; no newer UNCTAD completions vintage superseded the June insight this quarter.

The dashboard above is built as a Q3 layer stack: diverging vintage bars, completions???orders???backlog geography, steel share path plus H1 leaders, an order-versus-backlog scatter, July YTD aircraft race bars, and the held forge strip.

## The headline table: Aug prior vs Q3 print

| Metric | Prior (Aug update) | Q3 print | ?? |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| China ship order share (CGT) | ~52.2% of 2025 GT (derived) | **72%** of H1 2026 orders | **+19.8 pp** |
| Korea ship order share (CGT) | ~26.8% completions weight | **19%** of H1 orders | ???7.8 pp |
| China end-June orderbook (CGT) | ~60% (research-era approx) | **65%** (134.03 / 206.59) | **+5 pp** |
| Asia trio GT completions | **91%** of 2025 GT | **91%** | **held** |
| China crude steel share | **52.0%** (FY2025) | **~53.7%** (H1 2026) | **+1.7 pp** |
| India crude steel (H1) | 8.9% FY share | **9.3%** / **87.0 Mt** (+7.1% YoY) | +0.4 pp |
| Airbus share of A+B duo | **54%** (Cirium H1) | **53.2%** (July YTD) | ???0.8 pp |
| China VLCC dry docks (tracked) | ~62% | ~62% | **held** |
| Ultra-heavy forge shops | 6 | 6 | **held** |

Open **Vintage ??** and toggle **Moved only** versus **Held / flat**. The thesis of this update is not ???Asia stopped building.??? It is that the *forward* clock ??? new orders and backlog ??? **re-concentrates** toward China even as the *completions* clock still shows the milder 91% trio print from June.

## Ship layers: completions eased; orders re-tightened

UNCTAD???s June insight remains the official completions story: **91%** of 2025 GT came from the Asia trio. Country splits inside that trio were **derived** in the Aug update. Clarksons??? H1 2026 contracting print answers a different question: *who is winning the next wave of yard work?*

Global newbuilding orders rose **66% YoY** to **42.95 million CGT** across **1,481** vessels. Chinese yards took **31.00 million CGT** (**+113% YoY**) ??? **72%** of the half-year total. Korea won **7.97 million CGT** (**+60% YoY**) for a **19%** share. The gap between China and Korea in H1 order share is about **53 percentage points**. End-June backlog concentration is slightly less extreme than H1 orders but still China-dominant: **65%** of **206.59 million CGT**.

Why can completions show a softer trio share while orders scream concentration? Completions lag contracting by years. A 2025 GT residual that leaks to Europe (cruise/naval), Vi???t Nam, T??rkiye, and others does not imply those yards are winning the 2026 LNG and containership order scramble. Switch to **Ship layers**. The stacked view makes the three clocks visible on one canvas; the China-gap view isolates how far H1 orders and backlog sit above the ~52% completions weight.

Treat CGT order shares and GT completion shares as **related but non-identical** units. The directional story is robust: the newest forward print does not corroborate a Western merchant-yard renaissance.

## Steel: the midyear share rebounds even as China tonnes fall

World Steel???s June release is the second hard vintage. Reporting countries printed **931.5 Mt** in H1 (**???0.7% YoY**). China produced **500.0 Mt** (**???3.0% YoY**) ??? still almost **54%** of that reporting pool. Relative to the Aug update???s FY2025 **52.0%** world share, the midyear run-rate is **+1.7 pp**. India remains the growth counterweight: **87.0 Mt**, **+7.1% YoY**, lifting H1 share to **~9.3%**. The United States printed **42.8 Mt** (**+6.3%**); Japan was roughly flat; Germany bounced **+8.9%** off a weak base.

Toggle **Steel H1** between share, YoY, and million tonnes. The industrial-capacity implication is deliberately two-sided. China???s *tonnes* are still contracting year-on-year ??? the same direction as FY2025???s **???4.4%**. But the *share* meter snapped back toward the research-era **~54%** band because the rest of the reporting world also cooled. A midyear share rebound is **not** ultra-heavy forging capacity and **not** VLCC dock concrete. It does mean the feedstock geography for plate and sections looks *more* China-weighted at the half-year mark than the soft FY2025 annual print implied.

Open the steel share path: FY2024 **53.8%** ??? FY2025 **52.0%** ??? H1 2026 **53.7%**. The Aug update???s de-concentration headline survives as an annual fact; the Q3 run-rate refuses to extend it.

## Order vs backlog: China sits above the diagonal

Open **Order vs backlog**. Points above the 1:1 line won a larger H1 order slice than their end-June backlog weight. China is the extreme ??? **72%** of H1 orders against **65%** of backlog ??? which is what a surge vintage looks like when the orderbook has not yet fully digested the new contracts. Korea sits near the diagonal (**19% / 19%**). Japan and the residual rest-of-world sit below it: they hold more of the existing backlog than they are winning of the new flow.

This scatter is the cleanest answer to the brief???s core question for shipyards. Who still has the yards to build the next physical capital stock? On the *forward* CGT clock, the answer is more China-centric than the June completions insight alone suggested ??? even after the Aug update correctly booked a milder 2025 GT trio share.

## Aircraft July YTD: Airbus lead narrows, Renton still the tempo risk

OEM releases through July put Airbus at **418** commercial deliveries and Boeing at **367** ??? a duo total of **785**. Airbus???s duo share slips to **53.2%** from Cirium???s H1 **54%**. That is a small mix move, not a geography rewrite. Airbus remains behind a straight-line path to its ~**870** FY guide and will need the usual fourth-quarter ramp; Boeing???s July **53** handovers (including **39** 737 MAX units) keep the recovery print alive without yet proving a stable **42**/month MAX cadence.

For site-level FAL geography ??? which campuses actually assemble the jets ??? keep the [commercial aircraft FAL companion](/blog/commercial-aircraft-final-assembly-geography-2026) open. This update???s aircraft panel is a *tempo* print only: who is handing over more metal mid-year, not who poured new hangar concrete.

## What stayed frozen: docks and the six-shop forge club

Industrial-capacity commentary loves to extrapolate from order shares or steel tonnes into ???manufacturing power.??? The held layers refuse that leap. Tracked **VLCC-capable dry docks** remain China-heavy at ~**62%**. The ultra-heavy forge strip is unchanged: Japan Steel Works, Doosan, CFHI, Shanghai Electric???s heavy complex, Framatome/Le Creusot, and Sheffield Forgemasters. **North America still has no RPV-class member** in that inventory.

Open **Forges held**. Equal-weight shop counts are not throughput weights ??? JSW and Doosan matter more than the strip implies ??? but the *phone book* did not get a seventh number. Nuclear new-build, naval propulsion, and any industrial strategy that treats ???steel capacity??? or ???order share??? as synonyms for ???forging capacity??? still face the same bottleneck the [research map](/blog/heavy-industrial-capacity-research-2026) flagged.

Pair this update with [fiscal-industrial policy](/blog/fiscal-industrial-policy-update-202608) when the question is which incentives can touch yards and FALs rather than generic plant investment. Orderbooks and midyear steel shares move every half-year; dock concrete and certified ultra-heavy forges do not.

## Who is exposed ??? and what the delta actually buys

**Exposed to the wrong headline:** readers who treat the Aug update???s **91%** trio completions print as evidence that Chinese yard dominance is fading. H1 **72%** China order share and **65%** backlog say the opposite about the *next* delivery cohort.

**Exposed to frozen scarcity:** nuclear and naval programs that hoped a steel-tonne decline implied forge relief; shippers who assume dry-dock slots outside China/Korea are fungible; airlines whose delivery risk still clusters on a handful of FAL campuses even as duo YTD totals climb.

**What the delta buys:** a clearer separation between **three shipbuilding clocks** (completions, orders, backlog), a **midyear steel share rebound** against still-falling China tonnes, a mild **Airbus duo mix** trim, and unchanged **dock/forge** scarcity. China builds slightly less of the *last* GT pie than the 2024 research peak, is winning far more of the *next* CGT order pie, owns a rising fleet share from the prior ownership vintage, and still anchors docks and roughly half of world steel on a run-rate basis. India remains the steel growth story. The builder base for physical capital stock did not liberalize in Q3 ??? the forward prints say it tightened.

## Caveats and methodology

- **Sectors are not additive.** Do not average ship CGT order share with steel share into a fake industrial-capacity index.
- **Completions GT ??? order CGT ??? backlog CGT.** Clarksons uses compensated gross tonnage; UNCTAD???s trio print is gross tonnage completions. Direction travels; precise pp gaps across unit systems are approximate.
- **China/Korea/Japan completions weights inside the 91% trio remain derived** from the Aug update; only the trio total is disclosed by UNCTADstat.
- **H1 steel shares use World Steel reporting-country totals (931.5 Mt)**, not a fully reconciled world annual denominator ??? treat **53.7%** as a midyear run-rate, not a final FY2026 share.
- **Japan and rest-of-world order/backlog splits** outside disclosed China/Korea figures are residual estimates for charting.
- **Dry-dock and forge inventories are held** ??? absence of a new audited global registry is not proof that no individual yard expanded a dock.
- This post is a **vintage delta**. For the Aug completions/steel stack use the [prior update](/blog/heavy-industrial-capacity-update-2026); for the cross-sector research map use the [research ledger](/blog/heavy-industrial-capacity-research-2026); for GT concentration history use the [shipbuilding companion](/blog/global-shipbuilding-gt-delivery-concentration-2026).

## Bottom line

Versus our [August update](/blog/heavy-industrial-capacity-update-2026), the newest mid-year prints say the **forward builder base re-concentrated**: China takes **72%** of H1 2026 ship orders by CGT and **65%** of the end-June orderbook, while crude-steel midyear share rebounds to **~53.7%** even as China tonnes fall **3%**. Airbus???s July YTD duo lead narrows to **53.2%**. The scarce dock and forge layers remain frozen. Who still has the yards, dry docks, and heavy fabrication base to build the physical capital stock? On the clocks that moved this quarter ??? **China, more than the completions vintage alone suggested** ??? with Korea still the high-value yard counterweight and the West still missing from the ultra-heavy forge club.`,
